The use of botnet malware has become a major concern in the cybersecurity landscape, as it enables attackers to carry out malicious activities such as sending spam, hijacking accounts, and launching DDoS attacks. To combat this issue, researchers have developed various detection tools, including honeypots and intrusion detection systems. These systems collect data on suspicious activity and identify patterns indicative of botnet usage. To improve the effectiveness of botnet detection, this paper proposes a new method that leverages natural language processing techniques to analyze honeypot data. This approach involves identifying patterns in botnet command sequences and clustering IP addresses based on the commands they receive. To validate this approach, the researchers collected data from honeypots located within residential networks and trained a neural language model to generate a set of command patterns characteristic of botnet activity. Using this model, the researchers analyzed command sequences from the honeypots and identified groups of IP addresses based on their command profiles. To evaluate the efficacy of their method, the researchers conducted a comprehensive analysis of honeypot command logs, including a thorough examination of the command patterns they generated. This analysis revealed that the command patterns they identified were associated with a variety of malicious activities, including spamming, search engine hacking, identity theft, and hacking campaigns. Furthermore, the researchers found that IP addresses receiving commands from multiple patterns were more likely to be involved in malicious hacking campaigns. This analysis demonstrates the potential of their method for detecting botnet activity, and they plan to further develop and refine it in future research. This research contributes to the ongoing effort to develop more effective methods for detecting and mitigating botnet attacks. To facilitate future research, the researchers have made their command profile data publicly available. This research marks an important milestone in the application of natural language processing techniques to botnet detection. To the knowledge of the researchers, it is the first study to apply neural language models to identifying botnet activity. This analysis of honeypot command logs provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of botnet malware and highlights the potential benefits of using natural language processing techniques in this field. This thesis introduces a groundbreaking approach to visual object recognition within complex document images, combining the principles of layout analysis and object detection to identify and extract objects from diverse image backgrounds. A novel method for object representation, utilizing a bag of visual word model in both spatial and spatial-temporal contexts, facilitates the classification of retrieved objects, with our system capable of accurately extracting objects from dense, overlapping, and distorted data with high degrees of robustness and accuracy. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in various document image datasets, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art techniques under similar conditions. Furthermore, the versatility of our system is demonstrated through its successful application in two real-world commercial scenarios, the identification of payment slips and checks, with impressive results that are competitive with or even superior to those achieved by human experts. All related source code and associated datasets are publicly available on the following repository: https://github.com/kekechuo/DocVOR. Our proposed framework is designed to reduce computational and memory requirements by leveraging a novel gradient sampling approach, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through a range of experiments that showcase its ability to achieve state-of-the-art performance while improving efficiency and accuracy in large-scale video modeling tasks. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving superior performance on a range of large-scale video datasets while maintaining a significant reduction in computational requirements. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applications of our method in the fields of video classification and object detection, where it achieves impressive results and outperforms existing methods. Recent research has highlighted the limitations of abstractive summarization models, which often produce facts inaccurately. To overcome this issue, we've developed a novel approach that integrates a fact-checking module into the encoder's architecture. This module verifies facts during the summarization process by comparing generated tokens with reference summary tokens from their training data. Leveraging BERT's knowledge graph as a basis for existing knowledge, our model can identify errors and ensure factually accurate summaries. To further refine this process, we've established a dual objective loss function that penalizes incorrect facts while rewarding those that remain truthful. Furthermore, we've developed an adaptive penalty system, which adapts fact-checking sensitivity based on the summary's content. Through thorough experimentation on the SummEval dataset, we've demonstrated that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of factuality, producing more accurate summaries with greater coverage of source facts. Furthermore, we've shown that our model's fact-checking module can be repurposed to improve summary coherence by preventing the inclusion of irrelevant facts. We propose a new definition of coprimeness in discrete systems, which diverges from existing definitions that relied on irreducibility. Diverging from these established definitions, our concept of coprimeness is applicable to any discrete system, without the need for irreducibility. Key to our research is the identification of a specific subset of polynomials, known as the Rosenbrock polynomials, which form the basis of our primary findings. Firstly, we demonstrate that two discrete systems are mutually coprimimal if and only if their corresponding Rosenbrock polynomials are coprime, drawing upon a connection between discrete systems and polynomial ideals. Building on this foundation, we establish a critical equivalence relation, called weak-coprimality, which enables us to extend existing research on reachability and stabilizability in linear time-invariant systems to more general discrete systems, without the requirement of irreducibility. Furthermore, our work generalizes and expands upon multiple existing results, including those concerning the inner and outer Kukreja factorizations, the existence of a minimal polynomial set, and the properties of the Bezout matrix. Our research also reveals that the existence of a minimal polynomial set is an equivalent characteristic of coprimimal systems, providing a valuable computational tool in the form of a factorization algorithm that can be applied to any discrete system. Lastly, we demonstrate that the existence of a minimal polynomial set is also a necessary and sufficient condition for two discrete systems to be weakly coprimimal. Our research draws heavily from the existing literature on polynomial ideals, providing a unique contribution to this field. Ultimately, our work serves as a comprehensive treatment of this previously under-represented concept of coprimality in discrete systems. Recent research has focused on reducing the computational and memory costs of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by eliminating unnecessary filters, leading to promising results in the pruning of CNN filters. However, current methods have limitations as they rely on the assumption that network filters are uniformly utilized, a notion not supported by existing studies. This paper presents an innovative Self-Affinity-Matrix-based Filter Pruning (SAMP) method that leverages self-affinity matrices to assess the relationships among CNN filters and facilitate pruning. SAMP consists of three key components: Self-Affinity-Matrix Construction (SMC), Clustering (CLU), and Pruning (PRU). SMC generates self-affinity matrices to capture the relationships among CNN filters, while CLU groups filters based on their self-affinity matrices to form clusters. Clusters are then evaluated to determine the significance of each cluster's filter, and PRU eliminates less essential filters assigned to lower-ranked clusters. Experimental results on prominent CNN architectures demonstrate that SAMP outperforms state-of-the-art methods by achieving improved accuracy outcomes and reduced computational complexity on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets. Additionally, SAMP exhibits greater adaptability to various pruning ratios and surpasses previous methods in terms of runtime efficiency. annotations to gather detailed information about the pages, ultimately creating a large 
dataset of 1.67 million annotated entities. WikiGUM outperforms existing wikification 
databases in both entity categorization and comprehensive linking, offering a valuable 
resource for developing and evaluating Wikification applications.

WikiGUM annotations, achieving a 53.4% F1 score in entity linking and outperforming 

existing state-of-the-art models. To our knowledge, our model represents the first 

comprehensive Wikification model capable of integrating and combining various semantic 

attributes to identify and link Wikipedia entities. The model and dataset are available

Deep neural networks often struggle with understanding complex data, resulting in inaccurate predictions. This issue is exacerbated when the data is high-dimensional, making it difficult for the network to grasp important patterns. Our proposed solution, In-Training Representation Correlation (IRC), addresses this problem by incorporating correlation analysis into the training process. By doing so, it encourages the formation of clear, discrete patterns within the data, which are beneficial for model comprehension. We achieve this by incorporating a correlation module that promotes the emergence of robust patterns by eliminating redundant representations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of IRC, as it consistently outperforms baseline models across various domains. Furthermore, IRC is found to improve model interpretability by generating simple, discrete patterns within the data, while also producing more robust features that enhance classification and linear classification tasks. These features are also found to improve the performance of pre-trained models when fine-tuned. Notably, IRC is easy to implement and requires minimal modifications to existing neural networks, as it can be integrated into multiple layers with different objectives. A crucial component of visual navigation in autonomous vehicles is loop closure detection, which allows them to determine the relationship between past and present locations and update their position accordingly. To achieve this, a novel method is proposed that uses a two-way loop closure strategy, which not only identifies a vehicle's current location but also generates new keyframes and poses. To improve performance, a dynamic reference set is developed that filters out non-relevant images and selects only the most informative ones for loop closure detection. To handle the high number of potential matches, a dynamic scoring system is employed, which updates the scores of candidate images based on the similarity of their descriptors to the candidates in the reference set. As a result, a higher quality reference set is generated, which in turn produces more accurate candidate images and improved loop closure results. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing solutions, with a 33% increase in loop closure rate and 50% fewer incorrect matches. Furthermore, the method is shown to be effective in a challenging scenario involving a real-world road network with multiple similar-looking roads. Cache side-channel attacks have been a significant threat to software systems for years, compromising both software and hardware. While previous research has investigated hardware cache side-channel attacks, there is still a knowledge gap regarding software cache side-channel attacks. This study addresses this knowledge gap by introducing CacheQL, a novel language for identifying and analyzing cache side-channel attacks. CacheQL's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comprehensive ground-truth dataset of 12 applications, where it accurately detects cache side-channel attacks in 100% of cases. Additionally, CacheQL is shown to accurately trace the source of these vulnerabilities to specific lines of code in software. An evaluation of 12 production software libraries and APIs using CacheQL revealed that 11 of them, including Apache Commons Math3 and Google Guava, leak sensitive information due to cache side-channel vulnerabilities. Furthermore, CacheQL successfully identified the vulnerable lines of code in these libraries, which in some cases matched the locations identified by previous research. This study's results indicate that CacheQL is a powerful tool for identifying and locating cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software systems. This research focuses on developing control strategies for a group of vehicles to maintain a formation in the absence of a centralized coordinator. By considering the angular position of each vehicle's rotor axis with a reference point, the formation problem is redefined as an attitude synchronization issue. We then derive control algorithms that enable steady-state formation configuration and formation shape, allowing vehicles to adjust their distance from the reference point. By establishing stability criteria for this problem, we demonstrate the robustness of our approach to internal disturbances and measurement errors. Notably, our solution does not rely on the vehicles' relative velocities, a common requirement in previous solutions. Finally, we present simulation results to validate the efficacy of our control strategies. The effectiveness of image quality assessment algorithms for dehazed images is often evaluated based on the perceived differences between dehazed and original images, but this approach is limited by its reliance on available reference images. This paper introduces a new evaluation method that addresses this issue by developing a partial variation-based metric to assess dehazed images without requiring reference images. This metric is composed of two components: a partial variation component and a distortion component, both of which provide a more accurate evaluation of dehazed images. The first component measures the perceived differences between dehazed and original images, while the second component captures distortion in the dehazed images. Experiments show that the new metric outperforms existing metrics in evaluating dehazed images. This method is then extended to enable the evaluation of dehazed images in cases where neither the original nor dehazed image is available, which is known as the blind image quality assessment problem. This extension involves using a deep neural network to predict the perceived quality of dehazed images based on their distorted characteristics. The predicted quality scores are then used to evaluate the images. The new metric and the associated algorithm are tested on datasets of dehazed images and shown to outperform existing blind quality assessment methods. In this study, an innovative approach called Neural Payload Insertion is presented, enabling attackers to seamlessly embed a backdoor into a machine learning model. Diverging from conventional methods that modify the model's architecture or training data, this technique inserts a covert layer between the model and its output, rendering the attack difficult to detect. By combining this with a novel optimization objective, the attacker can successfully embed the backdoor. Notably, our research focuses on deep learning models, and we demonstrate that this technique can be applied to both CNNs and Transformers. Experimental results show that DeepPayload achieves a high attack success rate of up to 95% in real-world settings, and a remarkable 100% success rate in a controlled environment. Additionally, our research highlights the effectiveness of DeepPayload in launching devastating attacks on popular machine learning models, and we emphasize the importance of developing robust machine learning systems to counter the threat of such attacks. Deep neural networks have achieved impressive results in various medical survival analysis tasks, yet their predictions remain difficult for medical professionals to understand. This ambiguity hinders the growth of artificial intelligence in healthcare. To address this challenge, we propose a new framework called the Reverse Survival Framework (RSF), which is designed to clarify deep survival model predictions. By analyzing the predictions of these models, we can generate hypothetical scenarios that would influence a patient's survival probability, and then use real-world data to test the validity of these scenarios. In our experiments, the RSF framework helped to explain the predictions of two well-known deep survival models, resulting in significant improvements to their accuracy. To facilitate further research, we have developed an open-source Python package that can be used to build and explain deep survival models. This package, called PySurv, is available for free on the Python Package Index. Our goal is to make it widely adopted in the field, and we believe that it has the potential to revolutionize the development of deep survival models. By making it publicly available, we hope to take the first step towards integrating these models into clinical settings, where they can truly benefit medical professionals. Recent approaches have attempted to incorporate attribute information to improve re-identification, but these methods have been limited by their inability to account for attribute overlap and often rely on attributes that are not relevant to the identification task. The Large Hadron Collider has successfully produced a substantial amount of data, primarily consisting of proton-proton collisions. By converting these collisions into a mathematical representation, it's feasible to extract the underlying physics information. We have developed a sophisticated computational framework that leverages advanced mathematical techniques to extract the physical information from LHC data, specifically those indicating the presence of Dark Matter. This innovative approach has the potential to significantly enhance our understanding of the LHC's indicators of Dark Matter, ultimately enabling us to test theoretical models more effectively. Utilizing this framework, we have analyzed the LHC data, focusing on two key indicators: monojet and dilepton pairs with large missing energy, and derived the associated statistical distributions. Our proposed system integrates this strategy with a new routing mechanism to efficiently deploy optimal latency routes across large-scale networks, outperforming current standards managed by the Internet Engineering Task Force. The results indicate that it surpasses the state of the art in optimal latency routes, with significant benefits including reduced computational requirements and user-friendly configuration. These advantages enable network operators to quickly deploy optimal latency routes, facilitating a substantial reduction in latency. The results of our simulations also reveal a substantial decrease in the occurrence of suboptimal latency routes. In conclusion, our proposed system offers a practical solution for large-scale networks to achieve optimal latency performance. To speed up the processing of large, sparse tensors like those found in quantum chemistry, we've developed a vectorization technique that optimizes trace examination for dependencies within tensors. This approach, called Dependency Driven Trace Examination (DDTE), automatically identifies and utilizes relationships between tensor elements to break down complex matrix multiplication operations into smaller, more efficient components. DDTE's effectiveness is enhanced by its ability to adapt to various tensor structures and multiplication patterns, thereby maximizing the potential for speed improvements. The implementation of DDTE using OpenFIM compiler framework yields significant performance gains, leading to a 2-4 times improvement in runtime speed compared to existing sparse matrix codes and 5-10% increase in performance after vectorization, as demonstrated through its application to real-world tensors. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art sparse tensor tensor codes and is compatible with multiple programming models, including TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs. Additionally, we've analyzed the performance of DDTE on different platforms and identified key optimization opportunities for future development. The code for DDTE is available for public access. Microorganisms constantly interact with and affect their surroundings, and studying these relationships at a cellular level can provide valuable insights into their ecological significance. Although various methods exist for characterizing individual microbial cells, analyzing how these organisms interact presents a greater challenge. This is because each possible interaction involves multiple cells, and observing them all simultaneously is highly impractical. As a result, researchers often rely on limited data, such as images of small groups of cells, to make inferences about larger populations. Our research presents a statistical framework for analyzing these types of data, allowing us to better understand how different levels of resolution affect our understanding of microbial interactions. By applying this framework to simulated and actual data from Bacillus subtilis colonies, we were able to accurately predict the distribution of different cell behaviors. This demonstrates the potential for high-volume, multi-cell characterization to significantly advance our understanding of microbial interactions, and provides a foundation for further research in this area. Currently available tools, however, require explicit feature models for handling unsatisfiable parts of the specification. Our research aims to eliminate this requirement, achieving an unsatisfiable core calculation that incorporates all logic operators except Until. By modifying LTLf specifications, particularly adding a universal quantification, we can effectively identify the core of unsatisfiable parts using a k-bdd-based algorithm, thereby enabling the insertion of a negation-bound constraint. Our approach is further validated through successful testing on real-world case studies. Future directions for expansion include supporting additional LTLf operators and adapting the method to first-order modifications.

Autonomous driving heavily relies on accurate vehicle location recognition from LiDAR point clouds, which is often hindered by the immense point cloud density and limited vehicle-centric context. To overcome this, we introduce AttDLNet, a novel, efficient framework for precise 3D LiDAR location recognition. By leveraging a 3D Dilated Convolution Network (3D DLCN) to extract contextual features and an attention-based mechanism to distill critical vehicle context, AttDLNet generates informative vehicle maps. A center-based sampling strategy further enhances performance by incorporating vehicle-centric information. Notably, AttDLNet achieves remarkable results on NuScenes and KITTI benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art models in accuracy, while significantly reducing computational burden and memory usage. A key component in mechanical engineering, the rolling element bearing (REB), is prone to faults. To address this, a new fault diagnosis framework, built upon a temporal logic neural network (TLNN), has been developed. The TLNN learns fault patterns directly from sensor input data. To enhance its performance, a new approach to data pre-processing has been introduced, which involves extracting key features from the time domain, known as temporal features. These features are then used to train the TLNN. To evaluate its effectiveness, a comprehensive set of experiments was conducted using real-world data from the NRB and UHAB datasets. The results show that the TLNN-based method achieves high accuracy and fast computation times, even on large and complex datasets. Furthermore, its ability to learn from small datasets was demonstrated, showing its potential for use in applications with limited data. The TLNN also outperformed other state-of-the-art methods in this context. To further demonstrate its effectiveness, a real-world application was presented, where the TLNN was successfully integrated into a wind turbine data monitoring system to detect faults in REBs. The results showed that the TLNN was able to identify faults in the wind turbine blades, even when the machine was still operating. Overall, the TLNN has shown promising results in the field of fault diagnosis, and its unique architecture makes it well-suited for applications where data is complex and difficult to analyze. Facial animation relies heavily on synthetic 3D faces, which are essential for realistic motion. To achieve diverse and natural-looking motions, it's necessary to create a wide range of synthetic faces with varied textures and shapes. However, most current methods struggle to generate high-quality faces with specific textures or shapes efficiently. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach, which generates high-resolution, photorealistic 3D face models with diverse textures and shapes. Our method utilizes a novel neural network architecture, called Trunk-Branch Generative Adversarial Networks (TB-GANs), which consists of a common trunk network and multiple branch networks. The trunk branch learns to capture global facial structures and common features, while the branch networks specialize in specific textures or shapes. This allows for efficient and varied 3D face generation, resulting in improved sampling flexibility. To further improve the realism of generated faces, we also introduce a texture-aware image synthesis module. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our TB-GANs approach, which outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in generating high-quality faces with specific textures or shapes. Our TB-GANs models and face datasets will be publicly available to facilitate future research. This paper addresses a support vector machine scenario where communication among networked agents is restricted, with each agent relying solely on its local data. By utilizing a network's collaborative computational resources, we develop a novel primal-dual gradient flow method allowing each agent to derive its dual solution locally. Additionally, we establish the convergence properties of this method, demonstrating its convergence to a unique equilibrium point and convergence rate through stochastic approximation theory. Furthermore, inspired by ADAM's optimization strategies, we derive a modified gradient flow formula for the primal-dual framework and validate its generalization capabilities on a large network. Our findings are supported by a comprehensive set of numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world data. To facilitate further research, we provide a publicly accessible implementation of our proposed method in Python. As far as we know, this is the first study to explore large-scale support vector machine problems within a decentralized network context. Our primary contributions include the development of a novel primal-dual gradient flow method for distributed SV systems, a convergence analysis, and the application of stochastic optimization techniques to improve large-scale SV learning on large networks. This approach utilizes a unique property of deep networks where high-frequency features rapidly decay as they progress from early to late layers. To capitalize on this characteristic, we propose a new method that involves two stages. First, we create a disturbance in the early layers of the denoising network, which affects the details of the noisy input image. The output of this modified network serves as a refined feature representation that guides a denoising strategy in the subsequent stage. In the second stage, we leverage this feature representation to reconstruct a clean image by utilizing the network's later stages. The key advantage of our approach lies in its ability to enhance image quality using only noisy input images without requiring any clean images or prior knowledge of clean image distributions. Moreover, our method is highly efficient and can be easily integrated into existing denoising networks, resulting in improved performance. The impact of player fatigue on performance has been a longstanding concern in sports, yet it remains an underrepresented topic in research due to difficulties in measurement. We introduce a novel method for quantifying player fatigue, drawing from physiological measurements, and apply it to the NBA to examine its effect on on-court performance. Our player-level model, grounded in a dynamic game-theoretic framework, incorporates a player's current fatigue as a state variable and demonstrates that incorporating fatigue dynamics improves predictive accuracy by 1.9% in terms of R-squared and 0.06 in mean absolute error. Our model also accurately forecasts the likelihood of a team covering, a key concern for coaches and scouts. The player fatigue metric enables us to identify which factors, including age, position, minutes played, and points scored, have the most significant influence on fatigue. Notably, our results contradict the conventional notion that scoring tends to increase fatigue, revealing instead that fatigue is primarily affected by defensive intensity. Our method can be adapted to any sport, and our findings suggest that player fatigue is a crucial factor to consider when evaluating team strategies and player performance. Finally, we propose that the player fatigue metric could have practical applications in sports management and decision-making. For example, coaches and scouts can use this information to anticipate how players will perform in upcoming games after a prolonged rest period. To address this issue, we propose a novel method combining meta-filter and a vector operation to achieve high-performance tasks with even a single example. The proposed method, Meta-filter, is composed of a filter and an integrator. The filter is designed to produce a feature vector aligned with the task using a limited number of examples, while the integrator projects the task concept onto the filter output. This approach enables the model to dynamically align its feature representation with the task concept using a limited number of examples, effectively solving the few-example problem. Additionally, we propose a task knowledge augmentation technique to enhance the model's generalizability, which involves generating multiple task knowledge vectors from a limited number of examples and combining them using a probabilistic approach. This method allows the model to acquire a dynamic alignment of task knowledge from a limited number of examples. Recent advancements in medical image segmentation using Transformers have
yielded promising outcomes. However, the majority of current methods rely on a
standard Transformer model that processes all input features, resulting in an
inefficient process that leads to excessive computation and decreased
segmentation accuracy. To address this, a novel method called DAE-Former is
proposed, an attention-driven Transformer that effectively segments medical
images by focusing on the most relevant information. This is achieved through
two key modules: a feature selection module that identifies and filters
meaningful features from the input, and a segmentation module that uses these
selected features to produce accurate segmentations. Empirical studies on two
standard medical image datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the DAE-Former
approach, outperforming current methods in both segmentation accuracy and
computational efficiency. Notably, the use of the DAE-Former approach reduces
computational costs by up to 40%. Additionally, the approach is easily
scalable, allowing it to be applied to a broader range of medical image
segmentation tasks. The implementation of the DAE-Former approach is available
on the GitHub platform for public access. For further information, the

This research focuses on the characteristics of ions confined in quadrupole and hexapole ion traps.  The analysis begins with a mathematical representation of the perfect quadrupole trap, which is then used to determine the exact motion of an ion within a Paul trap.  The motion of the ion is described using a mathematical operator, which is then used to demonstrate the existence of coherent states.  The properties of these coherent states are examined, and the minimum required energy to prevent the ion from touching the boundaries of the trap is identified.  The study also explores the effects of introducing an additional harmonic potential to the trap, which can be used to rotate the ion.  Furthermore, the characteristics of ions confined in hexapole traps are analyzed, including the conditions necessary for ions to pass through or be blocked by the trap.  The research also examines the effects of energy fluctuations on ions in the trap.  The findings of this study are relevant to various fields, including mass spectrometry, atomic physics, the study of ion rings, and ion optics.  Additionally, the potential for using trapped ions to study the effects of rotation and the generation of spinors could be explored in the future.  The analysis also extends to the properties of trapped electrons.  Overall, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of ions in quadrupole and hexapole traps.  The study also highlights the potential for developing new types of ion traps that can be used to advance various fields.  Finally, the mathematical formalism developed in this study can be applied to other areas of physics, including the study of coherent states and the motion of particles in different environments.

Diabetic patients often develop complications that can lead to unforeseen outcomes compared to those without the condition, one such complication being the appearance of foot ulcers. These ulcers can become severely infected and in severe cases, result in amputation, highlighting the necessity for early detection. Early detection, in turn, requires accurate imaging technology to prevent unnecessary delays in treatment. This research aims to address this issue by developing a method that leverages deep learning techniques to enhance image quality and reduce noise, ultimately facilitating effective ulcer detection. Our proposed approach involves a two-stage process consisting of denoising and super-resolution, which we tested using various datasets and evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in improving image quality and enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted a comparative study to identify the optimal combination of pre-processing and super-resolution loss functions for our model. Our results show that the proposed approach outperforms other methods, achieving a high accuracy of 99.96%. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's ability to generalize to other datasets. Our research is significant as it addresses a critical challenge in diabetic foot health, with implications for early detection and treatment. This research has the potential to improve patient outcomes and reduce the need for amputations, ultimately benefiting individuals with diabetic foot conditions. Tangle 2.0, a proof-of-stake blockchain protocol, leverages a directed acyclic graph to achieve consensus through a distributed approach, enabling efficient transaction propagation. By focusing on the heaviest DAG in the network, Tangle 2.0 generates a single, consensus-driven path for transaction validation. Yet, previous analyses of the protocol's finality model in Tangle 2.0 revealed inconsistencies in transaction validation times. To address this, we developed a new metric called the longest path's root set, representing all possible consensus paths within the heaviest DAG. Furthermore, we established the Number of Confirmed Events Theorem, demonstrating the number of confirmed events within the root set correlates with the number of confirmed events network-wide. Based on this theorem's proof, we devised an algorithm to efficiently verify confirmed events within the root set and integrated it into the Tangle 2.0 implementation. The results show that the new verification algorithm reduces confirmation times to nearly zero, a significant improvement over previous analyses of the protocol's finality model. Moreover, our findings align with real-world blockchain performance observations. By introducing this verification mechanism, we aim to advance research into the properties of the Tangle protocol and contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics. Researchers have been investigating non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) as a potential solution to the limited available spectrum in future wireless networks. However, the increased interference in the downlink NOMA system poses a significant challenge to achieving optimal throughput. In the realm of active learning and active search, the primary objective is to locate a specific target item within a vast search space by dynamically querying its characteristics. This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm that leverages prior knowledge about the search space to significantly minimize the number of queries needed. Specifically, the algorithm assumes that the target is concentrated in a particular region of the search space and uses prior information to pinpoint its location. As a result, the algorithm achieves a substantial reduction in query complexity, achieving a time complexity of O(sqrt(d/lambda)) where d represents the maximum distance between the search space and the target, and lambda is a measure of how well the target is represented in the search space. Notably, when the target is known in advance, the algorithm can even achieve a time complexity of O(sqrt(n)). Finally, the practical efficacy of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated through a simulation-based experiment. Overall, the findings of this research underscore the benefits of combining quantum and classical approaches to address the challenges of exploration and learning. More broadly, the study contributes to the emerging field of quantum active learning and its potential applications. This is a foundational article on partial derivatives within the framework of non-smooth mathematics, with a focus on pointwise definitions and further development in [HLP20]. Within this framework, functions are defined at every point, even where they lack continuity or differentiability. This article establishes a natural, pointwise concept of partial derivatives for Baire-one functions, building on [He21]. It is shown that partial derivatives of Baire-one functions are themselves Baire-one functions, with implications for nearly every key theorem from real analysis in the context of pointwise differentiability. A notable exception is the Rademacher-Bernstein theorem, for which an alternative formulation is provided. Additionally, a detailed exploration of the differentiability of Baire-one functions is presented through various characterizations, with further developments in the companion paper [HL22]. A comprehensive appendix is provided to establish the Baire category of non-differentiable functions. This work is foundational to [HLP20], with a revised, streamlined version presented here. This paper develops initial findings on linear quaternion differential equations, an extension of linear system theory in quaternion parameter spaces. A key characteristic of linear quaternion differential equations is that their right-hand side satisfies a certain product property. By applying the Cayley-Hermite formula, a method is employed to transform these equations into systems of linear complex ordinary differential equations, thus allowing researchers to leverage established methods from linear complex ordinary differential equation analysis. The paper further explores essential aspects of linear quaternion differential equation theory, providing a foundational framework for future research. The reader is also encouraged to consult the author's related Ph.D. dissertation for additional information on this subject matter. To facilitate understanding, two appendices are included, offering an overview of the fundamental principles of quaternion algebra and providing counterexamples to illustrate the implications of omitting the product property in equation definition. The accompanying system theory chapter will also be available online. We developed the Echo Halls platform, a web-based tool utilizing a novel method of information dissemination through role-based simulated discussion. Our investigation focuses on how political discourse influences citizens' perception of and interaction with political figures. Our initial findings reveal that Echo Halls' design, which includes a political figure's personality, ideology, and party affiliation, has a significant impact on users' dialogue patterns, with more extreme figures promoting greater conversation among supporters. We observed that Echo Halls users tend to engage in discussions primarily with like-minded individuals, resulting in a 'bandwagon effect.' Furthermore, our analysis indicates that Echo Halls users' interactions are influenced by a'social influence' factor, with users often choosing to engage with figures from their own party before those from opposing parties. We discovered that Echo Halls users' opinions on politicians are influenced by their political views and party affiliations but not by their political ideology. Finally, our research reveals that Echo Halls users' interactions are driven by a 'homophily effect,' with users frequently joining parties based on their similarity in personality to other members. In federated learning, a central server combines local model updates from individual clients, 
which is particularly beneficial when data privacy is a concern. However, this approach often leads to 
a common model that may not perform optimally on specific client data. A solution to this issue is 
the creation of customized personal models, tailored to individual client requirements, but this often 
comes at the cost of increased communication and computation. This paper proposes a novel method to 
create personalized models with minimal additional computation and communication by using a 
hypernetwork that adapts a global model to a specific client's data distribution. We demonstrate the 
efficiency of this approach through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, including the 
MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. We found that this method successfully generates personalized models 
and achieves comparable performance to a fully trained model on a wide range of clients, using a relatively 
small number of iterations and minimal additional computation. We also observed that this method is 
particularly effective when the client data distribution is non-stationary, allowing the personal model to 
adapt to changing conditions. Furthermore, we observed that this method outperforms other approaches to 
personalized federated learning, including those utilizing meta-learning techniques. We also found that 
this method is resilient to changes in the underlying data distribution and can still produce accurate 
personalized models. This research has significant implications for real-world applications where data 
distribution is often dynamic. We hope that this work will inspire further research into the design of 
personalized models within the context of federated learning. Additional information, including the 
source code and experimental results, can be found on the following GitHub repository:

Recent breakthroughs in NLP have been largely driven by pre-trained models that
can handle diverse tasks, but their versatility comes at the cost of substantial
computational requirements. While knowledge distillation has been a key strategy for
reducing model complexity, most approaches focus on replicating task-level patterns
in the teacher model, which can be inefficient and lead to knowledge loss. In this
study, we propose a novel approach called LATTE, which focuses on transforming the
underlying workflow between multiple tasks to create a more efficient and effective
method for distilling knowledge. LATTE leverages a task-specific language path
that outlines the workflow between tasks, which can be learned during the pre-training
phase and utilized to enhance the computational efficiency of downstream models.
Through extensive testing on various tasks, including GLUE and PTB tasks, we have
found that LATTE outperforms previous distillation techniques in terms of its ability
to retain performance and reduce computational costs. The source code for LATTE is
publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhizeng97/LATTE. This research
presents a new paradigm for distilling knowledge, which can also be applied to
other areas of machine learning. The associated paper has been submitted to NeurIPS
2022. LATTE's potential for future applications in other areas is also explored.

A thorough analysis of simulation results highlights areas where current processor-based protection mechanisms fall short, while also providing a foundation for future processor development. Intelligent transportation systems heavily rely on advanced traffic forecasting models that can predict traffic states in real-time. The early prediction of traffic incidents is a critical concern for traffic management, particularly to prevent accidents, minimize travel times, and enhance passenger safety. This study introduces a dynamic, spatial-temporal focus network that can predict traffic incidents before they occur. The model utilizes a unique attention mechanism that combines historical traffic data with real-time information to identify patterns and predict incidents. The proposed method outperforms existing models in terms of both accuracy and speed, with a 10% improvement in overall performance and a 38% faster prediction time. The evaluation of an author's influence is crucial for deciding appointments, promotions, and awards. However, current methods primarily focus solely on individual papers, which leads to an incomplete picture of an author's overall contribution. We propose a new metric called Systematic Sample Size (SSM) to assess an author's influence by considering their entire publication portfolio. A study involving 400 researchers across various disciplines found that there is a significant variation in opinion regarding an author's influence. We discovered that high-impact authors are typically recognized by a larger number of peers, regardless of their field or citation counts. Furthermore, our research revealed that fields with limited research output tend to overemphasize individual contributions, while those with more publications have a wider range of influential authors. We also found that fields with a high rate of collaboration tend to have fewer authors recognized as major contributors. Overall, our study suggests that high-impact authors are often overlooked in their respective fields. We recommend using SSM as a fair and universal standard for evaluating an author's influence, complemented by other established metrics, which may help mitigate biases and inconsistencies. We also recommend that authors and their departments focus on promoting researchers who consistently produce influential work in their field. Finally, our research highlights the need for a standardized approach to assessing author influence that takes into account the complexities and variations across different disciplines. Unlike conventional methods, TIPS leverages a large dataset of paired natural language sentences and images to learn the connection between language and human poses. Unlike existing text-driven pose estimation techniques, TIPS does not require pose labels or specific training data. Instead, it utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate poses from text, eliminating the need for additional training. Our experiments demonstrate TIPS's superiority over previous state-of-the-art methods in pose estimation tasks, both in image-based scenarios and interactive applications. Current offloading systems, however, often rely on centralized resource allocation, disregarding users' personal IoT devices and limiting offloading opportunities, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these issues, we introduce Self-Managed IoT (SMIoT), a novel offloading system that empowers users to make informed resource allocation decisions across devices, allowing them to select the most suitable ones, offload tasks efficiently, and manage energy consumption. A proposed decision-making approach optimizes offloading for each task, balancing quality of service and energy expenditure. The effectiveness of SMIoT is validated through experiments using a realistic simulation and a proof-of-concept prototype. The results demonstrate that SMIoT yields up to 33% lower energy consumption and 29% higher quality of service compared to existing approaches, underscoring its potential to revolutionize personal IoT offloading. This ambiguity is resolved by the Poincaré invariant subset of states, which are determined by the field operators' expectation values for the Poincaré generators. Research has shown that Poincaré invariant states can be characterized by the field operators' expectation values, yet the physical significance of such expectations remains unclear. We propose a solution to this problem by suggesting that entanglement is a result of causal interactions between particles, and demonstrate that this approach is consistent with the Poincaré invariant states. The task of identifying films from given descriptions is a complex challenge within the field of film studies. Historically, film scholars manually classify films based on their literary analyses, but this process is time-consuming and requires extensive domain expertise. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring the potential of film studies research in data-driven film studies. This paper presents an approach to film classification that utilizes a given film description. We propose a model that can predict the film style based on the given text and further identify the film's production company. To this end, we have developed a multi-task learning model that jointly trains film style and production company prediction, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness on a large film dataset with impressive results. Additionally, our approach has been applied to a film retrieval task, and our results indicate that our model outperforms existing systems in film-style-based search. Ultimately, our research aims to lay the groundwork for a film studies knowledge graph and enable film studies research to be linked to film metadata. This will enable film scholars to leverage film studies research and analyze the evolution of film styles over time. By doing so, our approach can also be applied to other fields where film studies can be combined with other domains, ultimately creating a powerful tool for film studies and other interdisciplinary research. This study targets the sentiment recognition challenge at the 2022 Challenge on Sentiment Analysis in Dialogue (SAID) by modifying pre-trained models to classify dialogue speech into one of eight emotional categories based on two-second audio segments. Our proposed model, which incorporates a residual block with a multilayer perceptron for sentiment classification, achieved a high accuracy of 0.6899 in phase 1 of the challenge. Additionally, we further enhanced the model's performance by integrating it with speech enhancement techniques during the phase 2 submission process. Our resulting model, which utilized the enhanced speech features, ultimately placed third in the competition with an overall sentiment classification accuracy of 0.7096. By comparing pre-trained models with different architectures, we found that Resnet-18 outperformed others and served as a solid foundation for sentiment classification. Our results also confirm the effectiveness of utilizing speech enhancement techniques to improve the accuracy of sentiment classification in dialogue. Moreover, we successfully applied transfer learning to a new model, enabling it to learn from the features of pre-trained models and surpass those of standalone models. Furthermore, we utilized the attention mechanism to isolate key features from the pre-trained models and successfully integrated them into the sentiment classification model, ultimately leading to a high degree of accuracy in identifying emotions in dialogue. Our findings suggest that pre-trained models can be a valuable resource for developing more accurate emotion recognition systems. Ultimately, we found that combining pre-trained models with innovative techniques is a highly effective approach to achieving high accuracy in emotion recognition in dialogue. We examine how early matter domination affects the production of gravitational waves, focusing on the era following reheating. In this period, any initial density fluctuations will continue to impact the evolution of cosmic strings and loops, causing variations in the emitted gravitational wave power spectrum. This effect becomes more pronounced when the universe undergoes a transition from a radiation-dominated to a matter-dominated state, as the amplitude of the fluctuations increases by a factor of the ratio of the radiation and matter density. As a result, early matter domination enhances the production of gravitational waves, particularly in the more advanced universe where cosmic string networks produce significant distortions, leading to increased gravitational wave power. To illustrate this phenomenon, we consider a universe where an inflationary era ends with a matter-dominated era, followed by a thermalization period and a late-time phase of cosmic acceleration. Our analysis suggests that, under these conditions, gravitational wave experiments may be able to detect the distortions caused by cosmic strings. Moreover, we demonstrate that, in this universe, gravitational waves produced during the inflationary era are too weak to be measured by current experiments, but future experiments may be able to identify the distortions caused by cosmic strings. This finding implies that, in this universe, gravitational waves may be a valuable tool for reconstructing the properties of the inflationary era. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the early universe, where the matter and radiation densities may have been comparable, and suggest that, in this case, gravitational waves produced during the inflationary era may be more difficult to detect. However, we argue that, in this universe, gravitational waves produced during the inflationary era are not necessarily beyond the reach of current experiments. To illustrate this point, we consider a universe where an inflationary era ends with a radiation-dominated era, followed by a late-stage phase of cosmic acceleration. In this case, we demonstrate that, in this universe, gravitational waves produced during the inflationary era are within the range of sensitivity of current experiments. Furthermore, we show that, in this universe, the distortions caused by cosmic strings are more pronounced than in the case of early matter domination. This finding suggests that, in this universe, gravitational waves produced during the inflationary era are more easily detectable than in the case of early matter domination. In conclusion, we discuss the implications of our results for the study of gravitational waves produced during the inflationary era. Actuaries utilize actuarial factor models to analyze complex mortality patterns, which they break down into a few key underlying factors. Predicting future mortality relies on forecasting these factor dynamics. We compare and evaluate two approaches. The first involves stable factor relationships and focuses on forecasting the underlying factors themselves. The second model also accounts for factor interdependencies and simultaneously forecasts the factors and individual level factors. Our findings indicate that the latter approach, which considers the complex relationships between factors, provides more accurate long-term predictions. Nevertheless, we discovered that accurately forecasting the underlying factors themselves can be challenging. As a result, we recommend using factor interdependency-based models for forecasting, but with the factor contributions re-estimated to a common scale. This allows for improved short-term forecasting accuracy. Furthermore, we discuss the benefits and drawbacks of each approach and suggest future research avenues. A novel mathematical framework is introduced to represent assertions and their interrelations in formal systems, drawing inspiration from quantum mechanics. Within this framework, assertions can exist in states of truth such as true, false, indeterminate, and contradictory, with relationships between truth states defined by certain norms. Certain fundamental principles governing truth states are identified, and it is shown that a system of eight axioms is sufficient to define all possible truth states. It is demonstrated that this framework offers a more nuanced understanding of classical truth, with all classical truth states emerging as special cases of this framework's truth states. A discussion is presented to establish a connection between this framework and the measurement process in quantum mechanics. Finally, the framework's applicability is explored in the context of quantum computing and truth states, with potential implications for the development of a post-classical logic system. Abstract. A new mathematical framework is presented to represent assertions in formal systems, drawing from the principles of quantum mechanics. This framework considers assertions as vectors in a four-dimensional space, representing truth states, and defines relationships between these states using norms. Eight axioms are identified, which when applied to vectors in this space, characterize all possible truth states, and we show that this framework provides a more comprehensive understanding of classical truth as a special case. We also discuss how the measurement process in quantum mechanics can be related to this framework, and explore its applications in truth states, including post-classical logic systems and quantum computing. In this study, we examine the properties of low-rank optimal transfer, a fundamental concept in optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that the low-rank optimal transport distribution possesses unique asymptotic properties, and derive a consistent estimator for this distribution. Furthermore, our research reveals a notable phenomenon: the sample distribution of the low-rank transport cost converges at a rate of O_p(n^1/2), which contrasts sharply with the rate of O_p(n^1/4) observed for the sample distribution of the 1-Wasserstein distance. We also investigate and analyze the bias in estimates derived from the low-rank optimal transport cost, leading to the development of a debiased estimator that achieves significant improvements in bias reduction. Our theoretical findings are substantiated through numerical simulations and empirical analyses of both synthetic and real-world data. A key assumption underlying the multiple imputation method is that the imputation model closely mirrors the actual data generation model. When this assumption is breached, imputation effectiveness significantly wanes. This failure can occur if important variables in the data that influence the missing values remain unknown or if multiple variables with similar data patterns are used instead of a more concise representation of these variables. To mitigate this issue, users can either simplify their imputation model or employ dimensionality reduction techniques like principal component analysis to create a more streamlined model. This study examines the impact of using principal component regression on imputation performance and compares it to a basic linear regression model through simulations that demonstrate the benefits of this approach in challenging imputation scenarios. The results show that incorporating dimensionality reduction into imputation can substantially enhance its effectiveness. The research also reveals that while multiple imputation with reduced models may fall short of full maximum likelihood estimation in terms of mean square error, it outperforms the latter by reducing error variability. The study also provides an illustrative example of this approach in action using a real-world dataset. The research's findings are intended to encourage further investigation into the optimal balance between imputation model complexity and data representation in multiple imputation techniques. The goal is to facilitate active learning and exploration of how the topics learned in class impact students' daily routines. By analyzing Google Calendar data, students identify and record their involvement in various activities, which they then present in groups to address related tasks. Each semester, the students' output has been collected and found to produce valuable data that can be utilized for both academic research publication and future course refinement. We propose that this approach offers valuable insights into the curriculum's influence on students' time management habits and can also be applied to other educational settings. Moreover, the presented data offers a unique opportunity for reflective self-assessment, which may contribute to students' overall well-being. As a supplementary benefit, the project also fosters collaboration among students, which is a key aspect of the activity. Finally, a subset of the results are presented to demonstrate the potential applications of this approach in an educational setting. The presence of coronary artery calcium as detected by computed tomography scans 
is strongly linked to the occurrence of coronary heart disease, making it essential 
to measure it accurately and reliably. Traditionally, this assessment relies on 
quantifying the area of calcium deposits in coronary artery segments, but this 
method is often subjective and prone to variations. In order to address this issue, 
we developed a new method that leverages a combination of artificial intelligence 
and image processing to measure coronary artery calcium automatically and 
accurately. Our approach involves utilizing a series of image analysis algorithms 
to identify and process the coronary arteries, followed by a model that predicts 
the area of calcium deposits in each artery segment, allowing for a more precise 
and standardized measurement. To ensure the reliability of our method, we 
established a new benchmark by applying our algorithm to 1,000 high-resolution 
CT scans, resulting in a mean error rate of 12.0 mm^2 and a 90% agreement rate 
with expert assessments. Our results demonstrate that this new method is not only 
effective in identifying and measuring coronary artery calcium across a wide 
range of scans but also in detecting smaller calcium deposits that might be 
overlooked by human observers. Our open-source code and annotated dataset will 
facilitate further research and validation of this method, while also enabling the 
development of new image analysis algorithms that can improve the accuracy of 
coronary artery calcium measurement. By making these resources publicly available, 
we hope to motivate researchers to explore new approaches for enhancing the 
reliability and robustness of this assessment. Our ultimate goal is to establish a 
more precise and standardized method for measuring coronary artery calcium, 
ultimately leading to better patient outcomes. Our code and annotations can be 
accessed at https://github.com/UMBCVision/coronary_cca. To learn more about this 
research, please visit our project website at https://cca.um.edu. Our team invites

Utilizing the Spitzer space telescope and CHEOPS satellite, we successfully confirmed that this Jupiter does indeed occupy a nearly polar orbit, as required by its exceptionally short 1.18-day orbital period. This confirmation validates predictions made by planet evaporation models and satellite transit timing variations. Our research also reveals a possible reflection pattern on the dayside of MASCARA-1 b, which could be indicative of a cloud-free atmosphere with cloud reflections or a H/He atmosphere. Future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope may offer more insight into the atmospheric properties of this exoplanet. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining ground-based transit surveys with space-based transit and occultation observations in verifying planetary orbits and uncovering their atmospheric characteristics. Our findings also underscore the importance of multi-spacecraft collaborations in addressing the challenges of exoplanet detection and characterization. Ultimately, this research highlights the value of a multi-spacecraft network in uncovering the mysteries of exoplanetary atmospheres. We establish the existence of renormalized solutions

Notably, our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 74.45% for identifying all speakers and 69.79% for distinguishing genders in overlapping dialogue. Additionally, our experiments reveal that combining the gender classifier with the overall speaker identifier leads to significant improvements over previous results. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that WavLM pre-trained features significantly outperform those of wav2vec 2.0, resulting in a 1.5% increase for speaker identification and 3.21% increase for gender recognition. By doing so, TCRL enables agents to anticipate and respond to environmental changes before they occur, as opposed to simply learning from past experiences. In neutrino physics, a wide array of experiments have been conducted to study various aspects, but this report focuses on unconventional neutrino interactions, specifically those involving sterile neutrinos and non-standard model neutrinos. We examine the effectiveness of current searches and look at future prospects, particularly emphasizing the importance of the Muon Neutrino to Tau Neutrino Appearance Experiments, as well as searches for neutrino interactions involving photons, charged particles, and other exotic particles. Furthermore, this report delves into the interconnectedness between unconventional neutrino interactions and new physics beyond the standard model, specifically in the realm of Lepton Flavor Violation. Ultimately, this analysis aims to highlight key search areas for future experiments.

Due to the high magnetostriction anisotropy of these alloys, the saturation magnetization cannot be achieved uniformly throughout the entire grain structure. Results show that the saturation magnetostriction is highly dependent on the alignment of the grains and the orientation of the magnetic domains within the individual grains. Furthermore, the simulations reveal that the saturation magnetostriction exhibits a high degree of heterogeneity, even in the presence of a small number of grains. This heterogeneity is found to be particularly pronounced in the [100] orientation, where the orientation of the grains and the alignment of the magnetic domains within each grain can result in opposing magnetization directions. Consequently, the saturation magnetization can only be achieved partially, leading to a saturation magnetostriction of approximately 0.0015. In contrast, the saturation magnetostriction of the [111] orientation is found to be 0.0018, which is attributed to the alignment of the grains and the orientation of the magnetic domains within the individual grains. This value is found to be 2.5 times higher than that of the [100] orientation. This study provides a deeper understanding of the saturation magnetostriction properties of Terfenol-D and offers a new perspective on the alignment of the grains and the orientation of the magnetic domains within the individual grains. Building on established concepts, we establish that a finite implicit dimension corresponds to the presence of a finite set of generators. We explore the characteristics of this implicit dimension in various contexts, establish bounds for its value, and investigate its behavior in matrix algebras, as well as examine the specific case of the tensor algebra. Finally, we discuss the implicit dimension of the 4th Weyl algebra over a polynomial ring. In particular, we derive a lower dimension bound of 4 for any ring element, while demonstrating that any element with a degree of 2 or greater can generate the 4th Weyl algebra when the underlying ring is the integers. Conversely, we find that an element with a degree of 3 can generate the 4th Weyl algebra when the underlying ring is the rational numbers, but not over the polynomial ring. We present a new JavaScript library called json-metric-eval, which facilitates
the comparison of JSON data. This comparison can be based on multiple criteria,
including the similarity in information between two JSON files and the hierarchical
organization of key-value pairs within the files. The library allows users to
specify the exact configuration required for data comparison via command line
arguments or by editing a configuration file. This flexibility makes the library
suitable for use in quality control applications, enabling developers to assess
JSON files against predefined standards. The library supports the evaluation of
various metrics, including Levenshtein, Hamming, and Lempel-Ziv, and is capable of
processing JSON files of any size. Additionally, the library allows users to define
custom data similarity metrics for evaluating files against preconfigured
standard sets. The library is distributed under the terms of the MIT open-source
license and can be accessed via the GitHub repository at
https://github.com/boboas/json-metric-eval. A detailed description of its
installation and configuration procedures is provided on the library's wiki page.
We also discuss the library's potential applications in quality control and
provide a list of potential future extensions. The library's code and documentation
are available online, and we invite developers to contribute to its development. The
source code can be downloaded from https://github.com/boboas/json-metric-eval. A
binary version of the library is available for download at
https://github.com/boboas/json-metric-eval/blob/main/json-metric-eval-bundle.zip. The
library can be accessed via the npm package manager at
https://npmjs.org/package/json-metric-eval. The corresponding software
development kit (SDK) is available at
https://github.com/boboas/json-metric-eval-sdk. A quality control toolset is
available for download at
https://github.com/boboas/json-metric-eval-sdk/blob/master/examples/quality-control/.

By using this method, we have successfully mapped the ice fields in the Amundsen Basin, located within the Arctic Ocean, and found that they have been expanding rapidly over the last 20 years. This research has significant implications for understanding the Earth's climate system and has the potential to aid future research in this field. Go's lightweight concurrency model has made it a popular choice among developers for writing concurrent software. The language's primary strengths lie in its ability to manage complexity, offer strong safety guarantees, and provide an efficient concurrency experience. The Go team has effectively balanced control and abstraction in its concurrency API, allowing for high productiveness and adoption. Despite this, many Go developers are unaware of available tools to assess the quality of their Go programs, particularly those related to concurrency. This lack of awareness hampers the identification of potential issues, including those that could lead to catastrophic program crashes or data corruption. To address this issue, we introduce BinGo, a binary examination tool that analyzes a compiled executable to identify and quantify concurrency-related problems in Go programs. BinGo focuses on detecting data races, lock invocations, and LCK/MV programs, which are common and difficult-to-identify concurrency flaws. The tool leverages binary analysis, a novel approach to Go program analysis, to overcome the limitations imposed by the Go compiler. Through experiments involving 1,000 Go programs, we demonstrate BinGo's effectiveness in identifying concurrency issues, and its superior performance and accuracy over existing Go program analysis tools. Additionally, we provide case studies to highlight the practical applications of BinGo in Go concurrency program analysis. Predicting future pathways from videos is a complex task, yet it's crucial for tasks like autonomous driving and robotic manipulation. While existing models can predict a single, diverse outcome, they fail to produce multiple possibilities. To address this issue, we propose a new framework called Multi-future PredIctoR (MFP), which predicts multiple future paths. MFP is built upon the Multi-Stage GAN (MSGAN) architecture, which we modify to generate multiple pathways. We achieve this by transforming coordinate encoding to produce a grid, which serves as a template for multiple pathways. The grid is then transformed into a homogeneous space using affine transformations. To ensure the pathways are unique and diverse, we use a multi-scale feature fusion module. Furthermore, we propose a new evaluation metric called Average Intersection Ratio (AIR), which assesses the quality of predicted pathways based on average intersection ratio. Experimental results show that MFP outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of quantitative and qualitative assessments, including a new AIR metric. This research focuses on resolving the output consensus problem for nonlinear multi-agent systems with limited communication through a practical approach. Each agent is equipped with a state estimator that uses local sensor data and the output data of its two nearest neighbors. The transmission of this information, which is subject to data rate constraints, is facilitated by the agents themselves. We develop a state transition rule that ensures the stability of the state estimator and derive conditions for the transmission scheduling strategy that guarantee infinite-time output convergence and global stability. The proposed output consensus protocols are applicable to various nonlinear multi-agent systems, including those with different dynamics and sensing capabilities. A numerical simulation is used to demonstrate the practicality of these protocols for the output state fusion problem in a nonlinear multi-agent system with distinct dynamics. We also extend the results to address the output consensus problem for Lipschitz nonlinear multi-agent systems, with data transmission subject to data rate constraints. Theoretical results are supported by numerical simulations. The research findings are presented in three IEEE journal papers. The first paper deals with first-order nonlinear multi-agent systems, the second with discrete-time nonlinear systems, and the third with continuous-time systems. The latter two papers also consider the case of limited communication. The research findings are supported by numerical simulations. The main goal of the SNO+ water exposure is to constrain oscillation parameters by analyzing electron neutrinos from a carpooling experiment. However, an analysis was conducted to assess how neutron-proton capture events could impact this endeavor. By employing a Monte Carlo simulation, researchers found that these events could potentially be detected at a rate of one per million interactions. Furthermore, various nuclear reaction simulations were utilized to estimate the energy released during these captures, and it was determined that they would predominantly occur below 2.3 MeV. As a result, these events would likely blend in with the dominant background of 14C beta decay signals, and would therefore not significantly impact the measurement of oscillation parameters. In particular, these captures would not affect the determination of the oscillation maximum, the sign of the parameters, or the apparent distance to the neutrino source. In conclusion, neutron-proton capture events would have a negligible impact on the analysis of neutrino properties in the SNO+ water state. A detailed report on the simulation results and code used in this analysis is available at https://github.com/jamesdaly/np_capture, and an accompanying white paper will be formally published in a future journal issue. Please note that this analysis was conducted in a purely speculative capacity, as the SNO+ water exposure has already been ruled out due to the project's shift to salt. Nevertheless, this study could serve as a starting point for a similar analysis in the context of the JUNO salt exposure. Additionally, this research could be applied to any liquid scintillator project that involves detecting neutrinos, given the universal nature of the effects being considered. In the spirit of collaboration, this analysis has been made publicly accessible. For the benefit of other researchers who may be working on similar projects, an interactive web interface has been developed to visualize the simulation results and explore the implications of the analysis for the SNO+ water exposure project. Human conversations are highly personalized and informed by past interactions, leading to a surge in persona-based dialogue models that capture individual speaking styles. However, existing models have several limitations: they are trained on synthetic data rather than real-world conversations, overlook the importance of prior interactions, and struggle with adapting to new topics. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new persona-based dialogue model called TAILored Dialogue (TAILOR) that leverages real-world conversation data, incorporates knowledge from external sources, and utilizes persona characteristics to adapt its responses dynamically. The model's components are interconnected through persona-specific attention, allowing it to learn consistent persona traits. To demonstrate the effectiveness of TAILOR, we developed a new dataset that includes persona-based dialogue and knowledge sources, referred to as the MultiDomain Persona-Knowledge Dialogue Dataset. The results of our experiments show that TAILOR significantly outperforms existing models in multiple evaluation scenarios, including persona-based dialogue, knowledge-based dialogue, and open-domain conversation.
